items.prompt: Rewrite this line as a mental-status description of the appointment. Name the period observed, hold every sentence inside it, and where you keep a conclusion, write it as a conclusion with the observation it rests on. Then state one thing your version can no longer be used to claim.
items.stimulus: A fictional first appointment. The person arrived twenty minutes after the scheduled start and was then seen for 25 minutes. The observation log holds: apologised for arriving late; sat down without removing a heavy coat; answered every question in one or two words; three times said "I don't know" to questions about the last month; looked past the examiner towards the door for most of the appointment; twice asked how long the appointment would take; spoke at ordinary volume with no long pauses; stood up as soon as the examiner said the appointment was ending. The note written afterwards reads in full: "Late. Guarded, evasive, minimal engagement. Clearly did not want to be here."

answer.correct: A complete response names the 25-minute appointment as the period described, converts each of the three judgements into the observations behind them or removes it as unsupported, keeps any retained judgement labelled with its basis, and states a claim the rewritten version no longer supports. A workable version: "Seen for 25 minutes, having arrived twenty minutes after the scheduled start and apologised for the delay. Kept a heavy coat on throughout. Answered every question, mostly in one or two words, and said 'I don't know' to three questions about the last month. Looked towards the door for most of the appointment. Asked twice how long the appointment would take. Speech at ordinary volume without long pauses. Stood as soon as the ending was announced." The version no longer supports any claim about whether the person wanted to be there.
answer.summary: Name the period, replace the three graded adjectives with what was observed, and say what the honest version can no longer claim.
answer.reasoning: Guarded, evasive, and minimal engagement each grade the person against a standard the reader cannot see, and clearly did not want to be here is an unlabelled conclusion drawn from a coat, a door, and two questions about time. The observations behind them are all in the log and are barely longer written out. The last part of the task matters as much as the rewrite: an honest description gives up the claim about motivation, and a learner who rewrites the line while keeping that claim has changed the wording without changing the document.
acceptableResponses: A response may keep a labelled conclusion such as 'my impression was of reluctance, based on the coat kept on, the repeated question about length, and standing at once' provided the basis is attached.
A response may drop the apology or the volume detail as non-contributing, provided the three graded adjectives are dealt with.
Different orderings and different line headings are acceptable; some services group these observations differently.
commonErrors: Rewriting the adjectives into softer adjectives, so that guarded becomes reserved and nothing observable is added.
Keeping the conclusion about not wanting to be there and attaching only the lateness to it, which the log does not support once the apology is included.
Omitting the period observed, which leaves the description a statement about the person.
Adding detail that is not in the log, such as the person's tone or what they were thinking.

items.prompt: Which mood-and-affect entry is the defensible one for this fictional appointment?
items.stimulus: Across a 50-minute appointment the person laughed twice while describing a family argument, then wept for about a minute when asked about their job, then returned to laughing at the same subject. Both changes were large and quick. Asked how they had been feeling, they said: "Honestly, pretty good. Better than in years."

options.text: Mood: labile. Affect: labile, wide swings during the appointment.

Mood, in the person's words: "Honestly, pretty good. Better than in years." Affect: broad range with rapid, large shifts over the 50 minutes, including laughter while describing a family argument and about a minute of weeping about work, each change tracking the subject under discussion. The period the reported mood covers was not established.
Mood: elevated, though the person's account is unreliable. Affect: inappropriate.
Mood: not assessed. Affect: laughed twice, wept once.

answer.summary: Mood comes from the person and goes in their words; affect is described by range, the size and speed of each change, and the events behind it. Where the reported mood's period was never established, the description says so instead of grading the fit between the two.
answer.reasoning: The first option puts one word on both lines and so records a single judgement twice while appearing to record two things; it also assigns an observed pattern to mood, which nobody observed. The third replaces the person's report with the examiner's reading and adds a credibility judgement the encounter does not support. The fourth is honest about the observations and throws away a mood the person supplied on request, and it gives no range, so a later reader cannot compare it with anything. The second keeps the report in the person's words, describes the affect by range, intensity, speed, and the events behind it, and records the mismatch as a judgement a reader can check. Congruence is deliberately not keyed here: the reported mood covers an unstated interval and each observed change tracked its own subject, so the record's job is to describe both lines accurately and leave the relationship between them open for clarification.
commonErrors: Treating an observed pattern of expression as evidence about mood, which is the migration this lesson's second scene works through.
Reading a mismatch between report and observation as licence to overwrite the report.
Recording events without any descriptive summary, which leaves nothing for a later appointment to be compared against.

items.prompt: Select every phrase below that discards or distorts what was observed, so that a later reader cannot recover it.
items.stimulus: All five phrases come from notes about fictional appointments in which the following were observed: a person answered every question and gave the same account twice; a person was offered a leaflet and said no thanks; a person's appointment ran from 09:30 to 10:05; a person said they had been drinking most evenings and more over the past two months; a person paused for around eight seconds before each question about the past year.

options.text: Pauses of around eight seconds before questions about the past year.

answer.summary: Poor historian, refused, and alcohol excess each replace an observation with a judgement; the time and the pauses keep what was seen.
answer.reasoning: Poor historian deletes the consistency of the account and relocates the problem into the person. Refused reports resistance where a leaflet was declined, and the single verb invents a conflict for the next reader to inherit. Alcohol excess drops the amount, the direction of change, and the person's own account, and adds a threshold that nobody in the room set. The appointment times are compression that a reader can unpack exactly, and the pause description carries the event, its size, and the topic it attached to, which is what a later appointment can be compared against.
commonErrors: Selecting the appointment times because they are short, which confuses compression with the loss of information.
Leaving refused unselected because it seems factual, when declined is the word for what happened.
Leaving alcohol excess unselected because the person did describe heavy drinking, when the phrase still discards the amount, the change over two months, and the reason they gave.

items.prompt: Rewrite this description so that a clinician meeting the person in three months can use it. Name the period observed, separate mood from affect and attribute each correctly, replace every phrase that has discarded an observation, and finish with one sentence naming a question your version leaves open that the original had closed.
items.stimulus: A fictional review appointment. The observation log holds: appointment ran 11:10 to 11:40; the person arrived with a friend and asked that the friend wait outside; wore a coat and scarf indoors and said the building was cold; spoke quietly throughout, at ordinary pace, and was asked twice to repeat an answer; smiled once when the examiner mispronounced their surname and did not change expression otherwise; asked how they had been feeling, said "Same as before. Numb, mostly."; said they had stopped their evening walks in January and could not say why; asked directly about thoughts of not wanting to be alive, said there had been none since the last appointment and asked whether that would be written down. The note written afterwards reads in full: "Review. Flat affect, quiet, numb. Non-compliant with exercise advice. Nil SI. Brought a friend, sent them out. Unremarkable."

answer.correct: A complete response names the 30-minute period, records mood in the person's own words ("Same as before. Numb, mostly."), describes affect separately by what was seen (one expression change in thirty minutes, at the mispronounced surname; otherwise unchanged; narrow range) and marks any congruence statement as a judgement, replaces non-compliant with the observation (stopped evening walks in January and could not say why), replaces nil SI with what was asked and answered (asked directly, reported none since the last appointment, and asked whether it would be recorded), keeps the coat and the stated cold as an observation on its own line, and removes unremarkable. The closing sentence names a question the rewrite leaves open, such as why the walks stopped, or whether the quiet speech was new, or what the person's question about the record was about.
answer.summary: Name the period, split reported mood from observed affect, restore the four discarded observations, and say which question the honest version keeps open.
answer.reasoning: The original closes four questions at once. Flat affect contradicts an observed expression change and takes the person's word numb across into the affect line. Non-compliant converts a stopped habit with an unknown reason into a failure by the person, and deletes the January date, which is the part a three-month comparison needs. Nil SI records an absence where a question was asked, answered, and followed by a question of the person's own about the record. Unremarkable is a verdict that no later reader can check. The coat and the stated cold survive in neither version unless the learner puts them back, and they are the observation most likely to matter to someone asking a different question. The final sentence is the test of whether the learner has understood the trade: an honest description gives up conclusions in exchange for keeping questions available.
acceptableResponses: Different line headings and orderings are acceptable, since services organise the examination differently.
A response may retain a summarising word such as narrow range beside the observed event, and may note that one expression change in thirty minutes is a short basis for a range.
A response may treat the person's question about the record as belonging to the consent and documentation part of the encounter instead of the examination, provided it is not deleted.
Several different open questions are acceptable in the closing sentence, provided the question is one the original note had closed.
commonErrors: Keeping flat affect because the person used the word numb, which repeats the migration between the mood and affect lines.
Replacing non-compliant with a gentler judgement such as struggling with motivation instead of with the stopped walks and the unknown reason.
Writing denies rather than recording that the person was asked and what they said.
Dropping the coat and the stated cold as irrelevant, which is the observation a later reader with a different question would most want.
Ending with a summary of the rewrite instead of naming a question the rewrite leaves open.

criteria.description: Names the period observed and holds every sentence inside it.
Replaces each of the three graded judgements with the observation behind it, or removes it as unsupported.
States a claim the rewritten version no longer supports.
Selects the entry that keeps the reported mood in the person's words and describes the affect by range, change, events, and fit.
Selects poor historian, refused written information, and alcohol excess.
Leaves the appointment times and the described pauses unselected, distinguishing compression from loss.

rubrics.title: Integrated rewrite for a later reader

criteria.description: Names the observed period and organises the description into findable lines.
Records mood in the person's words and describes affect separately from what was observed, without carrying one across into the other.
Replaces non-compliant, nil SI, and unremarkable with what was observed, and retains the coat and the stated cold.
Names one question the rewritten version leaves open that the original had closed.
